nodes.content: Develop reinforcement learning transfer for robotic manipulation that reuses skills under hidden dynamics shifts while limiting negative transfer.
requirements: Match from-scratch success rates using 50% fewer target interactions when manipulation dynamics partially overlap.
On incompatible targets, stay within 5 percentage points of from-scratch success under equal interaction budgets.

nodes.content: Use online transition fingerprints to gate pretrained manipulation skills, falling back to a concurrently trained scratch policy when dynamics mismatch.
Can a 20-transition fingerprint detect incompatible gripper friction before pretrained skills cause negative transfer?
A 20-transition fingerprint detects incompatible gripper-friction shifts with AUROC ≥0.90, keeping gated success within five points of scratch.
Train contrastive fingerprints on source rollouts, calibrate the 20-transition gate, and measure friction-shift AUROC and success against scratch.
Evaluate 20-transition fingerprints on LiftGrip-v1 compatible and incompatible friction shifts, recording gate AUROC and equal-budget success versus scratch.
LiftGrip-v1 evaluation report with friction-shift labels, gate AUROC, and equal-budget success curves for gated transfer and scratch.
Audit LiftGrip-v1 report against episode logs, checking gate AUROC ≥0.90 and incompatible-target success gaps ≤5 points.
LiftGrip-v1 20-transition fingerprints achieved 0.93 friction-shift AUROC; incompatible-target success was 71% gated versus 74% scratch at equal budgets.
Reanalyze the LiftGrip-v1 report by friction severity and seed, testing AUROC ≥0.90 and incompatible-target success gaps ≤5 points.
On severe incompatible LiftGrip-v1 friction shifts, AUROC fell to 0.76; gated success was 58% versus 68% scratch.
Can five low-risk grip-slip probes identify severe friction shifts within the 20-transition gate budget?
Five low-risk grip-slip probes within 20 transitions raise severe-shift AUROC to ≥0.90 and limit scratch-relative success deficits to ≤5 points.
Reserve five of 20 transitions for low-force slip probes, retrain the gate, then benchmark severe-shift AUROC and success.
Using LiftGrip-v1 report baselines, test five slip probes within 20 transitions on severe shifts; measure AUROC and scratch-relative success.
Five slip probes raised severe-shift AUROC from 0.76 to 0.88; gated success was 62% versus 68% scratch.
Using report-defined friction bins, retest five probes on held-out LiftGrip-v1 seeds; measure severe-shift AUROC and budgeted success.
On held-out LiftGrip-v1 seeds, five-probe severe-shift AUROC reached 0.92; gated success was 66% versus 69% scratch.
Does seed selection explain why five-probe severe-shift AUROC differs between LiftGrip-v1 evaluations (0.88 versus 0.92)?
Five-probe gating meets both thresholds only on slip-rich seeds; fewer slip events explain the 0.88 AUROC and six-point deficit.
Replay both evaluations on identical seeds; stratify by observed slip events and compare paired AUROC and scratch-relative success.
Using LiftGrip-v1 report baselines, replay five-probe gating on matched seeds; stratify severe-shift AUROC and scratch-relative success by slip count.
Matched-seed LiftGrip-v1 slip-rich runs achieved 0.92 severe-shift AUROC and 66% gated versus 69% scratch success.
Using LiftGrip-v1 report baselines, regress five-probe detection errors and scratch-relative success on probe slip count, controlling friction severity.
Across matched LiftGrip-v1 seeds, probe slip count predicted neither detection errors (p=0.64) nor scratch-relative success (p=0.58).
Using LiftGrip-v1 report seed IDs, bootstrap paired five-probe AUROC and success differences across slip-rich and slip-poor severe-shift seeds.
Unadjusted LiftGrip-v1 bootstrap showed slip-rich AUROC 0.92 versus 0.86 slip-poor; scratch-relative success deficits were three versus seven points.
Defer slip-count-specific gating; prioritize severity-controlled validation because slip-rich seed gaps are unadjusted and slip count lacks adjusted predictive power.
Reuse pretrained manipulation skills only when their ensemble-estimated target advantage exceeds a scratch-policy confidence bound.
Can target-calibrated confidence bounds distinguish helpful pretrained skills from harmful ones before consuming half the scratch interaction budget?
Calibrate ensemble advantage bounds with 100 target transitions, then benchmark skill gating against scratch across compatible and incompatible shifts.
Train five Q-ensembles on LiftGrip-v1 rollouts; calibrate skill-versus-scratch advantage intervals with 100 transitions per target.
AdvantageGate-v1 checkpoint: five calibrated Q-ensembles, per-skill advantage bounds, and a scratch fallback policy for LiftGrip-v1.
Benchmark AdvantageGate-v1 on LiftGrip-v1 compatible and incompatible shifts, counting calibration transitions; compare success against half-budget and equal-budget scratch baselines.
On severe LiftGrip-v1 shifts, AdvantageGate-v1 reached 56% success versus 68% scratch at 2,000 interactions, exceeding the five-point limit.
Reject AdvantageGate-v1 for deployment: its 12-point severe-shift deficit exceeds the allowed five-point scratch-relative loss.
Train a scratch actor with source-skill imitation only when target gradients align, preserving scratch-only replay for fallback.
Can a 64-transition gradient-cosine gate select helpful skill imitation without slowing scratch learning on incompatible shifts?
Gating imitation at gradient cosine >0.2 matches scratch success in half the interactions on compatible shifts, with ≤5-point incompatible deficits.
Benchmark 64-transition, cosine >0.2 imitation gating on LiftGrip-v1: compatible success at half the scratch interactions; incompatible equal-budget gaps.
On LiftGrip-v1, gated imitation matched 74% compatible scratch success at 1,000 versus 2,000 interactions; incompatible success was 65% versus 68%.
Evaluate cosine >0.2 gating across held-out LiftGrip-v1 friction and payload shifts, measuring compatible interaction savings and incompatible scratch-relative success.
On held-out incompatible payload shifts, gated imitation reached 59% success versus 68% scratch at 2,000 interactions, exceeding the five-point limit.
Does transient positive gradient cosine on payload shifts explain the nine-point deficit, and would two-window agreement prevent it?
Transient positive cosine causes payload losses; requiring >0.2 across two 64-transition windows limits scratch-relative success deficits to ≤5 points.
Log consecutive cosine windows on payload shifts, enable imitation only after two positive windows, and compare equal-budget success against scratch.
Run two-window cosine >0.2 gating on held-out LiftGrip-v1 payload shifts; log false-positive imitation and 2,000-interaction success versus scratch.
Two-window gating reduced false-positive imitation from 21% to 8%; incompatible payload success rose to 66% versus 68% scratch.
Advance two-window gating to compatible-shift validation; it repairs payload losses, but its 50% interaction saving remains unverified.
Transfer source contact milestones as potential-based reward shaping, disabling shaping when target milestone predictions fail calibration.
Can target-calibrated contact milestones accelerate compatible-shift learning without misleading exploration under incompatible gripper geometry?
Calibrate source contact milestones; disable shaping above 15% target prediction error, then benchmark compatible learning and geometry-shift success.
Train contact-milestone predictors on LiftGrip-v1 source rollouts; calibrate a 15% error cutoff using 100 transitions per target.
ContactShape-v1 checkpoint with contact-milestone predictor, potential-based shaping weights, and 15% target-error shutdown rule.
Benchmark ContactShape-v1 on compatible friction and incompatible geometry shifts, counting calibration transitions; compare success against half-budget and equal-budget scratch.
ContactShape-v1 matched scratch’s 74% compatible success in 1,000 versus 2,000 interactions; incompatible geometry success was 65% versus 68%.
Stress-test ContactShape-v1 on held-out gripper geometries, measuring shutdown accuracy and equal-budget success against scratch across five seeds.
Across five held-out geometry seeds, shutdown detected 89% of incompatible milestones; ContactShape-v1 achieved 64% success versus 68% scratch.
Do the 11% of missed incompatible milestones cluster at extreme finger widths, risking success deficits above five points?
At finger widths >20% beyond source limits, missed shutdowns exceed 20% and ContactShape-v1 trails scratch by >5 points.
Sweep finger widths from source range to +30%; tabulate missed shutdown rates and paired success gaps by width bin.
Sweep ContactShape-v1 finger widths in 5% increments through +30%, measuring missed shutdowns and 2,000-interaction success versus scratch.
At +25% finger width, shutdown missed 24% of incompatible milestones; ContactShape-v1 success was 58% versus 68% scratch.
Audit ContactShape-v1 prediction errors at +25% finger width, comparing missed shutdowns with scratch-relative success across matched seeds.
At +25% finger width, four of five matched seeds lost 8–12 success points; missed shutdowns preceded failed grasps.
Restrict ContactShape-v1 to validated gripper geometries; compatible gains persist, but +25% width incurs a 10-point scratch deficit.
